title: The First Clerks (1994) Truly Gets Better With Age

commenti.body: I was a huge fan. Saw this in my local art cinema when it was released. But there was point maybe 15 years ago when a switch went in my head. Where dialogue I thought was brilliant became stilted and unfunny. Where characters I loved became dislikable pricks.  I think it was an accumulation of watching lots more Smith movies.  I built up an intolerance to his style.The problem now is even when I go back to watch his earlier work I now only see the irritation.

*Its a story that directionless teens and twenty somethings of any generation can relate to. No other film captures the timeless struggle of generation divide, sel- absorption, and being directionless of what one wants in life and what makes one happy then a film about two twenty something conveint store clerks.* 

This is a really good point about it.  

I'd say the same goes for the UK TV series Spaced which captured a similar directionless point of time. It was also the series that launched Simon Pegg and Nick Frost as actors and the director Edgar Write. It's dated in the same way Clerks has - in that it's innovations have been copied so much, they don't seem new anymore.

It's a time capsule 90's Gen X slacker movie, so I think it's ageless in that respect. 

It deserves an amount of advanced credit for what it is, basically a student film financed with credit cards and featuring armature to raw talent. The dialog is stilted that obviously reads better than spoken, but the jokes still mostly land. 

We watched Jaws with the kids last weekend and I can't help but to think salsa shark at the corresponding scene. The Death Star contractors is brilliant. It totally still resonates with anyone working a basic service job and having to deal with people and parts are still highly referential. I'm not even supposed to be here... This job would be great if it weren't for the customers... IN A ROW?!   
  
I watched the anniversary edition for the first time not long ago with the animated missing scene that was kind of neat.

When you're young, you relate with the trapped minimum wage worker who knows everything about star wars and little about anything else. 

The older you get, the more you realize that's precisely where the kid who knows everything about star wars and little about anything else belongs.

They have raw intelligence, but haven't utilized it for anything useful in an economy we are all required to participate in. You slowly learn that the world is full of people who are intellectually more capable than their current job.

I find the dialogue fine, but I COMPLETELY understand that others not enjoying it. I think the dialogue in how you described fits the tone of the movie, as it feels mostly natural to how young adults would exchange (as a tweny something myself, I feel how the dialogue is worded is raw for how me and my friends talk). You are spot on about the jokes. I am not sure, but Kevin Smiths' humor is something I aged out of as I got older but Clerks I still remains his funniest work.

Here is one of my favorite scenes: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zmA9alm-Pik](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zmA9alm-Pik)
This reads as so enlightened intellectual bullshit that I just can't help but roll my eyes, I'm sorry.

Absolutely adore the movie. It's interesting you discuss the ending, especially considering the original ending had Dante getting shot and killed. But due to this being such a downer Smith went back and rewrote it and shot the ending that is now in the film.
Neat. Articulate what's wrong with it.
Doesn't seem either enlightened or intellectual to me. Seems like solid older guy at the end of the bar perspective to me.
To be fair the intellectual tag is massive amounts of sarcasm.

Back in 2020 I revisited Kevin Smiths work for the first time since my early 20s and expected to hate it or have it age poorly.

 Clerks was a big surprise in that it was better than the first time I saw it and highly enjoyable.

I don't want to disagree as I hate when people make overblown statements like "I couldn't possibly disagree more blah blah blah" to dunk on someone's well thought out points, but I do feel almost the opposite, that it's only gotten worse with age and has become a dated relic of the era in which it was made. Specifically, rather than say something eternal about the ennui of a mid-20s existence, it seems to be remarking specifically on the angst of being a Gen X-er, and how they have it oh-so-much harder than any generation before, or ever will. Just the kind of rude snarkiness and being cruel for the sake of it, it's just not a popular thing any more for Gen Z or whatever and you get downvoted for saying things you'd be applauded for 30 years ago in this movie. I don't think the message was ill founded in its time or whatever, but it's bizarre how American Beauty is almost a punchline nowadays for the crime of talking about the upper middle class white boomer experience, while others are celebrated for talking about the slightly lower middle class white Gen X experience. They really controlled the pop cultural narrative for about 40 years there it seems.

A point that is eternal though that the movie isn't really making is the kind of entitled attitude of some workers in menial jobs who think the customers are shit and that they should bow before them just because the job sucks, while missing the point that they aren't putting any effort into the doing a good job in the first place. That part has aged like a fine wine

This comment reminds me why I think Clerks 2 is the better more profound film. Because of how it highlights a reality that many people in their 30-40’s are still trapped in the cycle of minimum wages work.
